# Introduction

With recent advancements in deep learning and computer vision [@meng2017IdentityAware; @li2022Deep], we now have accessible tools for detecting emotions from facial expressions. This has opened up new possibilities for studying the dynamics of emotional expression in various contexts, such as political speeches and public appearances of politicians. However, the large volume of publicly available videos and the specific nature of the data obtained by deep learning present challenges for analyzing such time series of emotional expression scores. This data is quite different from the data collected in ecological momentary assessment [EMA\; @tong2005Use] or experience sampling method [ESM\; @hoemann2020Contextaware].

Facial expressions of emotions are crucial aspects of human communication and have been extensively studied in psychology and other social sciences [@stewart2009Presidential; @mehu2015Emotion; @barrett2019Emotionalb]. The ability to accurately detect and analyze facial expressions of emotions has important implications for understanding human behavior and social interactions. Furthermore, the study of non-verbal and affective components of communication becomes an important part of political communication studies, especially with the rise of affective polarization and the increased frequency of emotional appeals by rising populist leaders [@widmannHowEmotionalAre2021; @martellaPopulismEmotionsItalian2022; @major2023Face].

The introduction of the FER2013 dataset [@goodfellow2013Challenges], which contained 30 thousand images of facial expressions with accompanying labels or categorizations of the emotion expressed in the image, brought forth the rise of deep learning methods based on Convolutional Neural Networks [CNNs\; @ezerceli2022Convolutional; @arriaga2017Realtimea]. These neural network architectures proved to be very capable of classifying images of facial expressions, and the accuracy of these models has been steadily improving over the years. However, the main limitation of this approach was that the categorization of detected emotions was inherited from the training data. This means that the majority of CNNs performed the so-called "7-Emotion Classification task" and returned the probability that the detected facial expression belongs to one of the seven categories: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise, and neutral facial expression [@wang2022Rethinking].

However, transformer-based neural network architectures have introduced the possibility of zero-shot learning, which allows for the classification of any given set of emotion labels without the need for additional training [@foteinopoulou2023EmoCLIP, @li2023CLIPER]. These advances have made it possible to study facial expression dynamics in a more nuanced and comprehensive way. The input for the transformer neural network is a set of images and a set of emotion labels, and the output contains an array of classification probabilities for each image. These probabilities can also be interpreted as the intensity of the detected emotion based on the detected facial expression (FER score). If the set of images is time-stamped and extracted from a video footage, then the resulting matrix of FER scores can be analyzed as a time series representing the dynamical system of facial expressions of emotions.

The aim of this paper is to provide a novel approach for modeling and understanding the dynamics of FER scores. This approach consists of several steps. We model the data-generating process of FER scores with a modified Damped Oscillator Model [DLO\; @boker2002Method; @boker2015Adaptive; @ollero2023Characterizing]. We use this model to perform a large-scale simulation with different parameters in order to obtain datasets resembling the ones that can be collected by applying zero-shot classification methods to process YouTube videos of political leaders and extract the time series of their FER scores. Next, we examine the performance of Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis (DynEGA) in assessing the dimensionality of the FER score time series and recovering the values of the latent dimensions using network scores. Finally, we provide a tutorial on how to simulate FER scores and how to estimate them from YouTube videos using the `transforEmotion` R package.

Our hope is that the simulation and tutorial will demonstrate the utility of facial expression recognition methods, especially zero-shot classification, in applied psychological research. By introducing a modfiied version of continous state-space DLO with a measurement model and its application to modeling emotion dynamics in political speeches, we aim to highlight the potential of this approach in understanding the temporal dynamics of emotional expression. Additionally, we will showcase the power of transformer-based neural network architectures in zero-shot image classification, which allows for the classification of any given set of emotion labels without the need for additional training. Furthermore, we will emphasize the usefulness of dynamic exploratory graph analysis (DynEGA) in assessing the dimensionality of emotion dynamics and uncovering latent factors in intensive longitudinal measures.

# Emotion Dynamics as a Damped Oscillator Model

How do politicians express emotions while delivering political speech? As public performances, political speeches are constructed, scripted, tailored to a specific audience, and aimed at influencing public opinion and political behavior [@sullivan1988Happy; @stewart2009Presidential]. Given these aims, we can expect that the emotional content of a political speech is not hectic, but rather follows a specific pattern. Political actors make emotional appeaals to the public and these appeals have shown to have significant effects on voter behavior [@crabtree2020It]. Strategic use of these appeals leads to the  the emergence of patterns of emotional expression produced by the process of emotional regulation, which is a process of changing from an existing expression of emotion to another desired expression [@tamir2016Why]. Politicians may downregulate emotions in situations where they want to prevent a specific emotion from lingering or escalating to extremes, and upregulate emotions in cases where the mobilization of a specific emotion may help achieve a current goal -- instrumental regulation [@kuppens2017Emotiona; @marcus2023Evaluating]. The interaction of these processes leads to the emergence of patterns in the expression of emotions.

The emotional content of political public perfomance can be divided into episodes of positive and negative sentiment. Sentiment exprsses the opinion of the politician with relation to the topic of their speech or public address [@dorle2018Political]. The use of positive and negative language and emotional expressions has been shown to be a tool at the disposal of politicians and they have been shown to exhibit a strategic use of the sentiment [@haselmayer2021Candidates]. This effect is highly prominent in the use of campaign messages to frame the state of the world in either a positive or a negative light [@crabtree2020It;@kosmidis2019Party]. But these arguments can be extended beyond the context of political campaigns, as political leaders are constanly engaged in public performances where they adress important issues and topic with emotional content. For example, in the first months of Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the emotional tone of Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky's public speeches was dominanted by negative emotions such anger, fear and sadness, while during the course of the conflict, his strategic use of sentiment led to more positive emotional expressions such as hope and joy in order to mobilize the public and boost morale [@nisch2023Invasion].

Based on these aspects of emotional content of political speeches, we model the dynamics of emotional with three latent variables: positive sentiment, negative sentiment, and neutrality. We propose a novel generative approach based on the DLO model [@boker2002Method; @boker2015Adaptive; @ollero2023Characterizing], named *Damped Linear Oscillator Measurement Model* (**DLO-MM**). The DLO-MM model has two main parts, one encompassing the dynamics of the latent trends generated using the DLO model, and the measurement part adapted from the direct autoregressive factor score model [@nesselroade2013dynamic; @golino2020modeling] that, combined, can be used to generate data mimicking emotional dynamics as measured with the intensities of the detected emotions in images and videos (FER score). Therefore, the resulting data generated using the DLO-MM model reflects the data structure of empirical FER scores that can be obtained using deep learning methods from images and videos.

We start by modelling the neutrality of the video $Nt$ following the approach of @ollero2023Characterizing and using DLO as state-space model in continous time. The same modelling strategy applies also latent score of positive and negative sentiment, $Ps$ and $Ng$. The dynamics equation of this model is a second-order differential equation that describes change of $Nt$ for an infitesmally small time interval $dt$:

\begin{equation}
\left[\begin{array}{c}
\frac{\mathrm{d} Nt}{\mathrm{~d} t} \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 Nt}{\mathrm{~d} t^2}
\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ll}
0 & 1 \\
\eta_{Nt} & \zeta_{Nt}
\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}
Nt \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} Nt}{\mathrm{~d} t}
\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{c}
0 \\
q_{Nt}(t)
\end{array}\right]
\label{eq:dlo-nt}
\end{equation}

Here, $Nt$ is the latent variable the captures the level of neutrality of the expression, $\mathrm{d} Nt / \mathrm{d} t$ is the rate of change of neutrality at any given time point of the political speech. Furthermore, we have $\mathrm{d}^2 Nt / \mathrm{d} t^2$, which is the acceleration of the rate of change of neutrality. Together they provide complete information about the neutrality of the facial expression at any given point of time and the upcoming changes in the neutrality of the expression after that point of time.

The key elements of the first component of the DLO-MM model are three cofficients which govern the dynamics of the latent score. We will call parameter $\eta_{Nt}$ the *lability* parameter. Negative values of this parameter tell us that the neutrality of the speech is in a stable equilibrium, meaning that the further the score of neutrality is from the equilibrium, the greater the acceleration it experiences to get back to the stable state. For example, if we have negative $\eta_{Nt}$ and if the neutrality of the speech is at a very high level, the acceleration will be negative, meaning that the neutrality will decrease and the speech will become more emotional. On the other hand, if the neutrality of the speech is at a very low level, the acceleration will be positive, meaning that the neutrality will increase and the speech will become less emotional. However, in case of positive values of this parameter, the neutrality of the speech will be in an unstable equilibrium, meaning that the further the score of neutrality is from the equilibrium, the greater the acceleration it experiences to move away from the stable state. For example, if the neutrality of the speech is at a very high level, the acceleration will be positive, meaning that the neutrality will increase and the speech will never incorporate any emotional content.

The parameter $\zeta_{Nt}$ is the *stiffness or resillience* parameter. It governs the changes in the amplitude of the oscillations. For example, if the neutrality of the speech is at a low level (bottom of the oscillation) and it moves back towards the equilibrium state, this parameter determines the amplitude of the next oscilation. Negative values of this parameter tell us that the amplitude of the oscillations will decrease over time, while positive values of this parameter tell us that the amplitude of the oscillations will increase over time. Thefore, negative values correspond to the resillience of the neutrality and the ability of a political to not show emotions during a political speech.

Finally, $q_{Nt}(t)$ reflects the influence of the content of the speech itself on the neutrality of the expression. Presumably, it's much harder for politician to stay neutral while discussing topics of war and human casualities, than it is to stay neutral while discussing tax service reform. In this way, we have two parameters which are specific to the rethorical skills and features of the political leader: their their affective-rhetorical style (stable vs unstable equilibrium) and their skill in instrumental regulation of facial expression of emotion (resillience); and one parameter refering to the content of the political speech. The influence of the speech content is estimated as a function of time $q_{Nt}(t)$ and it's also called the dynamic error of the DLO model. The dynamic error is assumed to be normally distributed with mean zero and variance $\sigma_q^2$. This dynamic error is what pushes latent score away from the equilibrium state, produces oscilations and "forces" eta and zeta parameters to govern the reaction of the system in the attempt to move back to the equlibrium state or push even further away from it.

Equation \@ref{eq:dlo-nt} is also used to model the latent score of negative and positive emotions: $N_g$ and $P_s$. The interpretation of the model parameters is very similar to the one we've provided for the case of neutrality, only in reverse direction as more neutrality implies less emotionality. It's important to note that we model the neutrality latent score in order to generate the baseline of affective dynamics and the overall (non)emotionality of the political speech. We simulate positive and negative sentinemt and then scale them so that the sum of the scores of all three is one. Therefore, the neutrality score is used for scaling purposes and it's not directly related to the measurtement model. It has an indirect influnce, because when the neutrality is high, the scores of all observable variables will be low.

Figure \ref{fig:dlosim} shows simulated trajectories of latent scores for two hypothethical scenarios. Top rows show a situation of stable neutral equilibrum where political leader shows a neutral facial expression for the entire duration of political speech (represented here with 300 frames). In the left panel, we see a gray line representing the trajectory of neutral expression, while the purple line represents indentical trajectories of positive and negative emotions. These are the idealized version of the trajectories, representing general tendencies without oscillations smoothed out  and without any source of error.  On the right panel, we have trajectories with the same parameters but with dynamical error of the DLO model introduced to the model. In terms of $\eta$ and $\zeta$ parameters, we have one set of parameters for the neutrality score and another one for the emotion scores. For neutrality, the combination of parameters shown in the top panels represents have high resillience and relatively stable equilibrium of neutrality score and a lower resilience, but much more stable equilibrium of emotion scores.

In the botom panel, we have a set of parameters that produces a relatively relatively stable expression of positive emotions, with low neutrality score. The speech beings with a neutral tone but quickly it shifts to the expression of positive emotions. We also see that during the course of speech there is a gradual increase in the expression of negative sentiment as well. This type of dynamics is the result of lower resillience of neutrality and relatively stable equilibrium. Lower resillience means that once it's pushed away from the starting position by the dynamic error, it converges to new equlibrium state of lower score. On the other hand, emotion scores have lower stability and higher resillience which means they are not heavily influenced by the dynamic error which enables them to experience longer periods of constant growth, followed by relatively stable episodes with just minor oscillations around their equilibrium state.

The second element of the DLO-MM data-generating model is the measurement part used for generating the observable FER scores. We modify the approach used for simulating observable variables from the direct autoregressive factor score model [DAFS\;@nesselroade2013dynamic;@golino2020modeling] and simulate the observable positive and negative emotions with the following steps. First we generate the matrix of factor loadings $\mathbf{ \Lambda}$ with 2 latent factors: positive and negative sentiment and $k$ variables per factor, in a total of $p$ variables ($p = 2\times k$). As stated before, the neutrality score is not included in the measurement model and it serves as baseline for affective dynamics and it used for scaling purposes. When neutrality is high, positive and negative emotions are not sufficiently salient. However, when neutrality is low, positive and negative emotions are being expressed.

In the second step the measurement error matrix is generated following a multivariate normal distribution with mean zeros and $p \times p$ covariance matrix $Q$, where *p* is the total number of variables ($k$ number of variables per emotion times two emotions: positive and negative). Finally, the observed variables $\mathbf{Obs}_{t}$ at time $t$ $(t = 1, 2, ..., N)$ are calculated using the following equation \ref{eq:dafs}. 

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{Obs}_{t} = \mathbf{\Lambda} \times \mathbf{X}_{t}^{T}+\mathbf{e}_{t},
\label{eq:obspos}
\end{equation}

where $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ is the factor loading matrix ($p \times q$), $\mathbf{X}_{t}^{T}$ is the transpose of a $q \times 1$ vector of latent scores at time frame $t$ generated using the DLO model, and $\mathbf{e}_{t}$ is a $p \times 1$ vector with measurement errors following a multivariate normal distribution with mean zeros and covariance matrix $Q$.  

The steps of the data generation mechanism can be summarized as follows. First, we obtain the latent scores of the emotions using the DLO model. Then, a factor loading matrix where each of the $q$ variables has a loading to its respective emotion equal to $\lambda_i' = \lambda + U(-0.15, 0.15)$ is created. Here $\lambda$ is a predefined fixed value for the loadings and $U(-0.15, 0.15)$ is a random noise drawn from a uniform distribution between -0.15 and 0.15 for each observable. This way, we introduce some variability in the factor loadings because when we have, for example, episodes of high negative sentiment that can be driven by one or two dominant negative emotions, while others are not as prominent. The loadings are then scaled so that the sum of the loadings for each latent factor is 2, creating a ceiling effect and differentiating the dynamics of specific emotions.

To further differentiate observed emotion scores, we add small noise to the predefined measurement error variance $\sigma^2_r$ for each observed variable, ranging between -0.01 and 0.01. Therefore we construct a diagonal $p \times p$ measurement error variance matrix $Q$, where each of the $p$ elements on the diagonal is equal to $\sigma^2_r + U(-0.01, 0.01)$. Again, this increases the range of the error variance for the observable variables as we expect that some emotions are harder to detect and more prone to misclassification. Then, Equation \ref{eq:obspos} is used to compute the observable scores for each variable, at time frame $t$.

The main aim of the proposed data-generating process using DLO-MM is to produce data that resembles the data obtained by applying zero-shot image classification methods to process YouTube videos of political leaders and extract the time series of their FER scores. We will illustrate this approach OpenAI's CLIP transformer neural network model [@radford2021learning].

The CLIP model is trained on a larger number and wide variety of images with natural language supervision that is abundantly available on the internet. By design, this model can be instructed in natural language to perform a great variety of classification benchmarks without directly optimizing for the benchmark's performance. This capability is similar to the "zero-shot" capabilities of the GPT large language model. Regarding text, modern pre-traning methods based on large web-scale collection of text has surprassed the benchmarks of the approaches based on high-quality crowd-labeled NLP datasets [@brown2020language] and CLIP was developed as a similar approach for computer vision. The model has been pre-trained on a huge dataset of 400 milion pairs of image and text (dominantly image captions) collected from the web and the model is able to learn to perform a wide set of tasks which includes OCR, geo-localization, action recognition and many others [@radford2021learning]. We utilize this model for facial expression recognition by using the following procedure.

Any application of CLIP is based on providing one or several images and a set of text labels as input. We will illustrate this approach by using images which represent frames from a public adress of Boris Johnson acting as UK's Prime Minister, published on the official YouTube channel of the Conservative Party, titled *Boris Johnson's Brexit Address to the Nation | This is not an end, but a beginning* [^1]. The entire video has 5331 frames and we sampled 350 frames, extracting taking every 15th frame of the video. This was done using the `transforEmotion` R package [^2]. Details about using CLIP for emotion recognition are available in the tutorial section of this paper.

[^1]: Video available at: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hdYNcv-chgY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hdYNcv-chgY).

[^2]: Downloading the entire video, extracting image and performing zero-shot facial expression recognition on 350 frames takes 169 seconds on an average laptop computer without a dedicated graphics card. The `transforEmotion` package can be installed from: [https://github.com/atomashevic/transforEmotion](https://github.com/atomashevic/transforEmotion).

# Representing Emotion Dynamics as Dynamic Networks (in the individual and population level)

The data generated using the Continuos State-Space DLO with a Measurement Model part or computed via zero-shot classification can be analyzed using Dynamic Exploratory Graph analysis [DynEGA; @golino2020modeling], that estimates a single network per individual (or per video), and a population network for all individuals (or all videos). **DynEGA** combines techniques from dynamical systems [i.e., time-delay embedding and generalized local linear approximation\; @glla2010] and exploratory graph analysis [@golino2019investigating; @golino2017ega1] -- a network psychometric approach for dimensionality assessment and reduction. The *DynEGA* technique can be used to estimate dynamical communities (e.g., latent emotions) in (intensive) longitudinal measures at different levels of analysis (individual, group and/or population).

Network models have been proposed in psychological research for decades [e.g.,\; @boker2018; @cattell1965; @guttman1953image]. More recently, a number of developments in network modeling in psychology originated a new area termed *network psychometrics* [@epskampNetworkPsychometrics] that relies mostly on the Gaussian graphical model [**GGM**\; @lauritzen1996graphical]. A GGM can be obtained by modeling the inverse of the variance-covariance matrix (and standardizing it to obtain partial correlations) in a way that non-zero elements are freely estimated [@epskamp2018gaussian], generating a sparse model of the variance-covariance matrix [@epskamp2017generalized]. As @epskamp2018gaussian note, inverting and standardizing the variance-covariance matrix won't lead to partial correlations that are exactly zero, meaning that the GGM is saturated. Regularization techniques, such as a variant of the *least absolute shrinkage and selection operator* [**LASSO**\; @tibshirani1996lasso] termed *graphical LASSO* [**GLASSO**\; @friedman2008glasso], are generally used in network psychometrics [see\; @epskamp2018gaussian; @epskamp2018tutorial].

<!-- The GLASSO is a technique that is very fast to estimate both the model structure and the parameters of a sparse GGM [@epskampggm]. The most used network estimation approach in psychological research (termed *EBICglasso*) is implemented in the `qgraph` package [version 1.4.1\; @epskamp2012qgraph]. The `EBICglasso` function [@epskamp2012qgraph] samples 100 logarithmically-spaced values of $\lambda$, following @foygel2010extended. The ratio range of $\lambda$ can be set by the user (defaults to 0.1). $\gamma$ controls the severity of the model selection (defaults to 0.50). The tuning parameter ($\gamma$) is used control the preference for complex models using the extended Bayesian information criterion [EBIC\; @chen2008ebic]. The *EBICglasso* has been shown to accurately retrieve the true network structure in simulation studies [@epskamp2018tutorial; @foygel2010extended; @williams2020back; @williams2019nonregularized].  -->

Network psychometrics on cross-sectional data has progressed into dimensionality assessment, where networks are estimated using the GGM or other network techniques [see @golino2019investigating] and an algorithm for detecting communities in weighted networks [Walktrap\; @pons2006walktrap] is used to identify latent factors. @golino2017ega1 called this approach *exploratory graph analysis* (**EGA**). Simulation studies have found EGA to perform as well as the most accurate factor analytic method, parallel analysis, and produce the best large-sample properties of all the methods evaluated [@golino2017ega1; @golino2019investigating]. 

In (intensive) longitudinal data, EGA can be used, but instead of using the variance-covariance matrix of the raw data, it uses the variance-covariance of $m$-order derivatives. The resulting network structure (GGM of the $m$-order derivatives) conveys information on how variables are *changing* as a function of time. As a result, the communities identified using the Walktrap algorithm reflect not simple, static factors, but dynamical factors of nodes that are fluctuating similarly as a function of time. @golino2020modeling called this technique the *dynamic exploratory graph analysis* (**DynEGA**), merging network psychometrics, dynamical systems modeling, and dimensionality assessment into a single framework that can estimate structures at the individual or group/population levels. 

DynEGA starts by transforming the time series of each observed emotion $V = \left\{v_1, v_2, ..., v_N\right\}$ into a time delay embedding matrix $\mathbf{X}^{(n)}$, where $n$ is the number of embedding dimensions. As pointed by @golino2020modeling, a time delay embedding matrix is used to reconstruct the attractor of a dynamical system using a single sequence of observations [@takens1981detecting; @whitney1936differentiable], preserving the phase-space dynamics of the system. In the time delay embedding matrix, each row is a phase-space vector [@rosenstein1993practical]:

\begin{equation}
X = \left[X_1 \mbox{ }  X_2 \mbox{ } ... \mbox{ } X_M\right]^\prime,
\label{eq:rowtme}
\end{equation}

where $X_i$ is the state of the system at discrete time $i$ and is given by:

\begin{equation}
X_i = \left[x_i \mbox{ }  x_{i+\tau} \mbox{ } ... \mbox{ } x_{i + (n-1)\tau}\right],
\label{eq:coltme}
\end{equation}

where $\tau$ is the number of observations to offset successive embeddings (i.e., lag or reconstruction delay) and $n$ is the embedding dimension. The time-delay embedding matrix is a $M \times n$ matrix, where $M = N - (n-1)\tau$ and $N$ is the number of time points.


**BIG FIGURE: latent + measurements + dynega + network scores**

<!-- 
Suppose that $U_1$ represents a column in a given dataset, depicting the time series of variable V1 from $t = 1$ to $t = 10$, with $U_1 = \left\{5, 6, 7, ..., 14 \right\}$. It's important to note that the values in this example significantly exceed typical psychology data. Nonetheless, this example serves the purpose of illustrating the mechanics of time delay embedding. The transformation of the time series $U_1$ into a time delay embedding matrix with five embedding dimensions and $\tau = 1$ results in the following matrix:

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{X}^{(5)} = \begin{bmatrix} 
5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & 9 \\
6 & 7 & 8 & 9 & 10 \\
7 & 8 & 9 & 10 & 11\\
8 & 9 & 10 & 11 & 12\\
9 & 10 & 11 & 12 & 13\\
10 & 11 & 12 & 13 & 14\\
\end{bmatrix} 
\quad
\label{eq:X}
\end{equation}

Once all the time series (columns) in the dataset have undergone transformation into a time-delay embedding matrix $\mathbf{X}^{(n)}$, it becomes possible to estimate derivatives using the Generalized Local Linear Approximation [@deboeck2009using; @glla2010].

Once the time series of each variable collected in an (intensive) longitudinal study and transformed into a time-delay embedding matrix $\mathbf{X}^{(n)}$, derivatives can be estimated using generalized local linear approximation [**GLLA**\; @deboeck2009using; @glla2010]. Derivatives can represent different aspects of change such as the rate of change or velocity at which the variable is changing over time (first-order derivatives) and the speed of the rate of change or acceleration (second-order derivatives).

@deboeck2009using and @glla2010 show how derivatives can be estimated in the GLLA framework:

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{Y = \mathbf{X}L(L^{\prime}L)^{-1}},
\label{eq:deriv}
\end{equation}

where $\mathbf{Y}$ is a matrix of derivative estimates, $\mathbf{X}$ is a time delay embedding matrix (with $n$ embedding dimensions; to simplify the notation, $\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}^{(n)}$), and $\mathbf{L}$ is a matrix with the weights expressing the relationship between the embedding matrix and the derivative estimates. The weight matrix $\mathbf{L}$ is a $n \times \alpha$ matrix, where $n$ is the number of embedding dimensions and $\alpha$ is the (maximum) order of the derivative. Each column of the weight matrix is estimated as follows, considering the order of the derivatives going from zero to *k*, $\alpha = [0, 1, ..., k]$:  

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{L}_{\alpha} = \frac{[\Delta_{t}(v-\bar{v})]^{\alpha}}{\alpha!}
\label{eq:weights}
\end{equation}

where $\Delta_{t}$ is the time between successive observations in the time series, $v$ is a vector from one to the number of embedded dimensions (i.e., $v = [1, 2, ...n]$), $\bar{v}$ is the mean of $v$, $\alpha$ is the order of the derivative of interest, and $\alpha!$ is the factorial of $\alpha$. -->

After estimating the derivatives for all time series (i.e., all variables), EGA is used to estimate the individual networks (one network per individual or per video). In this process, each matrix of derivatives will generate a different network and dimensionality structure (represented by clusters of nodes in the network) for each individual. The population structure can be estimated by stacking the derivative matrix of each individual (i.e., row-binding the matrices) and applying EGA to the stacked matrix. In both cases (i.e., individual or population structures), the resulting clusters in the networks corresponds to variables that are changing together [@golino2020modeling].

<!-- An example illustrates how this technique works: Suppose we ask three people to answer eight items of depression once a day for 100 days. After applying DynEGA to the data, we would obtain three important types of information (see Figure \ref{fig:Fig1}): the derivatives for the eight variables, the network structure for each person (intraindividual), and the network structure of the two people combined (interindividual). The left side of Figure \ref{fig:Fig1} shows the time series of first-order derivatives while the network structure of each individual are at the center (top and bottom represents subject one and two, respectively). The interindividual network structure is depicted in the right side of Figure \ref{fig:Fig1}. Note that we are omitting the community membership information to make the plot easier to visualize (each node has the same color as their respective time series of first-order derivatives). As can be seen in the network structure of person one (top network at the center of Figure \ref{fig:Fig1}), the pair of nodes pink and green are not connected (i.e. there is no edge linking these pairs of nodes). However, the same pair of nodes are connected in the network structure of person two (middle network at the center of Figure \ref{fig:Fig1}) and person three (bottom network at the center of Figure \ref{fig:Fig1}), and in the between-individual network structure (or population network) depicted at the right side of Figure \ref{fig:Fig1}. Additionally, the network structure of persons one and two clearly shows that the eight depression items form two groups or communities, while the network structure of person three forms four groups of two nodes each. # Simulation Design

To verify the suitability of ..., a Monte Carlo simulation is implemented. Four data conditions were systematically manipulated: sample size (50 and 100), number of variables per factor (4 and 6), number of factors (2, 3), error (0.125, 0.25, and 0.50 -- each one squared in the measurement error covariance matrix), and dynamic factor loadings (0.4, 0.6, and 0.8). 

The sample sizes were selected to reflect moderate (N = 50) and high (N = 100) samples, consistent with many empirical papers using an intensive longitudinal measurement design that typically don't use data from more than 100 individuals [@liu2016dynamical; @schmiedek2020training]. In terms of the number of variables per factor, three are the minimum required for factor identification [@anderson1958]. In the present simulation, the number of items were selected to reflect adequate (4) and slightly overindentified (6) factors [@velicer1976map; @widaman1993common]. However, in one condition was not possible to have an adequate factor identification for the *not equal* data structure, since the primary group of simulated data consisted of two factors, each comprising four items, but the secondary (distinct) group featured four factors, each with two items only.

The measurement error covariance matrix had $0.125^{2}$, $0.25^{2}$ and $0.5^{2}$ in the diagonal, representing low, moderate, and high errors. This strategy allows for the impact of the other variables systematically manipulated in the simulation to be better understood. The dynamic factor loadings of the *DAFS* model were selected to reflect small (0.4), moderately high (0.6), and high (0.8) loadings. Two conditions were held constant: the matrix with autoregressive (0.8) and cross-regressive coefficients (0), and the covariance matrix for the random shock (off-diagonal = 0.18; diagonal = 0.36). The values of the autoregressive and the cross-regressive coefficients and the random shock matrix were selected following @nesselroade2008dfm. 

Together, 216 conditions are tested, with all possible combinations of sample size (N = 50 or 100), variables per factor of the main group (NVAR = 4 or 6), number of factors of the main group (NFAC = 2 or 3), variables per group of the secondary group for the "NotEq" condition (NVAR2 = 2, 3, 4, or 9 depending on NVAR and NFAC), number of factors of the secondary group for the "NotEq" condition (NFAC2 = 2, 3, or 4, depending on NVAR and NFAC), loadings (LOAD = 0.4, 0.6, or 0.8),  EII method (weighted, unweighted, or edge list), and error (0.125, 0.25, 0.5).

## Data Generation

In the Monte Carlo simulation, 500 data matrices were generated for each combination of variables (number of factors, number of variables per factor, factor loading, and sample size) according to the DLO Model. Implemented in package ...

<!-- The measurement error matrix is estimated following a multivariate normal distribution with mean zeros and $p \times p$ covariance matrix $Q$, where *p* is the total number of variables (number of variables per factor times $F$). Finally, the observed variables $\mathbf{Obs}_{t}$ at time $t$ $(t = 1, 2, ..., N)$ are calculated using the following equation \ref{eq:dafs}. 

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{Obs}_{t} = \mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{F}_{t}+\mathbf{e}_{t},
\label{eq:dafs}
\end{equation}

where $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ is the factor loading matrix ($p \times q$), $\mathbf{F}_{t}$ is a $q \times 1$ vector of factors at time $t$, and $\mathbf{e}_{t}$ is a $p \times 1$ vector with measurement errors following a multivariate normal distribution with mean zeros and covariance matrix $Q$ [@nesselroade2008dfm; @nesselroade2002].  

Data following the DAFS model can be simulated using the `simDFM` function of the *EGAnet* package [version 2.0.2\; @EGAnet].

After all individual data is simulated using the DAFS model (as described above), they are combined into a single data file (row bind). Each data file with all the individual data corresponds to a replicate *i* (from 1 to 500) of a condition *j* (from 1 to 216). The DynEGA method is used to estimate a single network structure per individual and a population structure for all individuals (replicate *i*, condition *j*). Because the data from each individual comes from the same population model (the DAFS model) with the same number of items per factor, same number of factors, and same factor loadings (as defined by the condition *j*), the corresponding weights for each individual network will be similar, but not the same. Therefore, for the "Eq" condition, all individuals will have the same structure in terms of number of factors and number of variables per factor, but the estimated network weights vary from individual to individual, to the random variation of the data generation process. -->


## Data Analysis

**Accuracy, correlations** **R packages, ggplot2, transforEmotion**

In our current simulation, we assess the performance of three ergodicity information index methods, each computed using distinct prime-weight encoding strategies. The *unweighted* method utilizes prime-weight encoding derived from the adjacency matrix of individual networks (i.e., layers within the multiplex network). The *weighted* method employs prime-weight encoding computed from the network weights, while the *edge list* method utilizes only the edge list of the prime-weight encoding.

Within the simulation, we generated data for two sets of individuals under the direct autoregressive factor score model. In the first set, all individuals shared an equal number of factors, known as the "Eq" condition, enabling the representation of these individuals with a single population structure. In the second set of conditions, half of the subjects matched the "Eq" condition, while the other half exhibited a different configuration with varying factors, resulting in the "NotEq" condition.

We compared the three ergodicity information index methods (*unweighted*, *weighted*, and *edge list*) based on their *hit rate* or accuracy. A score of one was assigned each time the ergodicity information index yielded a lower value for the "Eq" condition (all individuals sharing the same dimensionality structure) compared to the "NotEq" condition (two subgroups with different dimensionality structures). This score indicates the accuracy of the ergodicity information index in identifying the set of individuals for which representing them with a single population structure is reasonable, as opposed to a set where such representation leads to a loss of information. The conditions used in the simulation were compared in terms of the mean accuracy of the ergodicity information index methods (*unweighted*, *weighted*, *edge list*). The partial eta-squared effect size is also computed for each condition and their combinations, in order to identify which impacts the accuracy of the ergodicity information index the most.

We also examine the average ergodicity information index values for both the "Eq" and "NotEq" data conditions. Additionally, we assess the mean difference between the ergodicity information index values estimated in the "NotEq" data condition and those in the "Eq" condition. Positive differences indicate instances where the new index is accurate, while negative differences signal situations where the index proves to be inaccurate.
